notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes from the sources found. Denominational notes are included where differences emerged in the retrieved material.

---

## Exodus 21 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — "These are the ordinances that you are to set before them"

- The Hebrew word *mishpatim* ("ordinances" / "judgments") refers to civil laws given as precedents to guide Israel's magistrates in cases of civil dispute. These are not abstract ideals but case-law for judges. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill notes these are "judicial laws respecting the civil state of the people of Israel… founded on justice and equity" and distinct from the Ten Commandments, being given through Moses as mediator rather than directly by God's voice. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott explains "judgments" means "the rules which shall guide judicial decisions." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- Precept Austin stresses that these laws are an "exposition" of the Ten Commandments (especially the last six, governing horizontal human relationships), and are meant to prepare Israel to live as a holy nation among the pagans. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-21-commentary)
- Adam Clarke (quoted by Enduring Word): "These different regulations are as remarkable for their justice and prudence as for their humanity. Their great tendency is to show the valuableness of human life." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)

### v. 2 — "If you buy a Hebrew servant, he is to serve you for six years. But in the seventh year, he shall go free without paying anything."

- All sources agree: this is not the chattel slavery of the modern era but indentured servitude, typically entered through poverty or debt. The six-year limit was unique in the ancient Near East.
- Enduring Word (David Guzik, citing Spurgeon): "Moses did not institute slavery in any shape; the laws concerning it were made on purpose to repress it, to confine it within very narrow bounds, and ultimately to put an end to it." He calls the Hebrew servant "more properly an 'indentured labourer', bound for six years" (quoting Cole). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: the servant was sold "for his theft" through the Sanhedrin, and his six-year term was absolute; the master was also required to furnish him liberally at release (Deut 15:13-14). Gill sees a typology: the servant's bondage pictures slavery to sin, and his free release pictures the liberty Christ gives "freely without money, and without price, of pure free grace." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott: "This law was an enormous advance upon anything previously known in the slave legislation of the most civilised country, and stamps the Mosaic code at once as sympathising with the slave." He notes that even Christianity 1,500 years later did not venture on so complete a social revolution. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: The Law did not create slavery; it regulated an existing institution and prohibited its abuse. A Hebrew could become a slave only through poverty (Lev 25:35-39) or crime (Ex 22:3). Freed slaves were to be given provisions from flock and field (Deut 15:12-14). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-21.html)
- Precept Austin (George Bush): "'Buying an Hebrew servant' may as legitimately imply the buying him from himself, that is, buying his services, as any other mode of purchase." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-21-commentary)
- G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Precept Austin and Enduring Word): the condition of slaves among the Hebrew people "would be in marked distinction to slavery as existing among other peoples. It was the beginning of a great moral movement." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-21-commentary)

### v. 3 — "If he arrived alone, he is to leave alone; if he arrived with a wife, she is to leave with him."

- Enduring Word: "At the end of the six years the servant went out with what he came in with." "By himself" is literally "with his back" — i.e., bare back, nothing more. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: If he came unmarried, he left unmarried. If he came with an Israelite wife, she went out with him — she was not the master's property. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott: the privilege of the married slave extended also to his wife and children if they entered servitude together. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

### v. 4 — "If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master, and only the man shall go free."

- The wife given by the master was presumably a foreign (non-Hebrew) perpetual slave. Enduring Word (citing Cole): "The wife was presumably a perpetual slave, and therefore the master's own property." This seems harsh to modern readers but reflects that the master had property rights in his own female slave. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: the wife was a "Canaanitish woman," given specifically to breed slaves for the master, and the marriage was not a full lawful marriage but a secondary arrangement. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott: If the Hebrew slave was unmarried when he entered service and was given a foreign slave-wife, she and the children remained in the slave condition when he left. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- **Keil & Delitzsch** (cited in search results): this was "an equitable consequence of the possession of property of slaves at all." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-21.html, via excerpt)

### vv. 5–6 — "But if the servant declares, 'I love my master and my wife and children; I do not want to go free,' then his master is to bring him before the judges… pierce his ear with an awl… he shall serve his master for life."

- All sources treat this as the "bond-slave" ceremony — a voluntary, life-long commitment motivated by love, not debt.
- Enduring Word (David Guzik): This foreshadows Christ, the willing bond-slave of the Father. Psalm 40:6 ("My ears You have opened") is seen as a Messianic reference to this ceremony. Jesus took the form of a bond-servant (Phil 2:7). The pierced ear also foreshadows the nail that fixed Christ to the cross (citing F.B. Meyer). Paul in Gal 6:17 speaks of bearing "the marks of the Lord Jesus" — like a branded slave. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: The servant was brought "unto the judges" (*Elohim*, meaning the Sanhedrin or court). The boring of the ear "denotes the strict and close obedience of such a servant to his master." He notes the Targum of Jonathan specifies it was the right ear. The servant served "for ever" — i.e., until the Jubilee. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott: "In order to mark that henceforth the volunteer bondman became attached to the household, he was to be physically attached to the house by having an awl forced through his ear, and then driven into the door or door-post." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- **The Expositor's Bible Commentary**: St. Paul rejoiced that his choice of Christ was beyond recall, "for the scars on his body marked the tenacity of his decision" (Gal 6:17). Paul remembered that a Hebrew could incur lifelong subjection "only by a voluntary wound, endured because he loved his master, such as he had received for love of Jesus." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/exodus-21.html)

### v. 7 — "And if a man sells his daughter as a servant, she is not to go free as the menservants do."

- Enduring Word (citing Kaiser): "Refers to a girl who is sold by her father, not for slavery, but for marriage." She was sold into a household with the expectation of eventual marriage to the master or his son. Therefore she was not released after six years like male servants — her status depended on the marriage arrangement being honoured. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: This concerns an Israelite father selling his "little daughter" (under age 12) through poverty. She did not go out in the seventh year, nor through loss of a tooth or eye like Canaanite servants, but through redemption, signs of puberty, Jubilee, or the master's death. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott: The father's right to sell children was part of ancient *patria potestas*, but rare among Hebrews. Women sold this way could claim freedom at six years if they chose (Deut 15:17), but if sold for marriage, they had additional protections. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary**: "She was not freed after six years like other slaves, but neither could her master sell her to a foreigner if he no longer wanted her." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-21.html)

### v. 8 — "If she is displeasing in the eyes of her master who had designated her for himself, he must allow her to be redeemed. He has no right to sell her to foreigners, since he has broken faith with her."

- Enduring Word: If the master chose not to marry her or give her to his son, the contract was considered breached. She had to be allowed to be redeemed — bought back by her family. She could not be sold to foreigners (or even to another Israelite outside the family, according to some commentators). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: "Then shall he let her be redeemed" — her father (or she herself, or a relative) could redeem her. The master had "dealt deceitfully with her" by breaking the marriage promise. He could not sell her to "a strange nation" — meaning to another Israelite of a different family, since the right of redemption belonged to her family alone. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott (alternative reading): The Hebrew may read "who hath NOT betrothed her." The master, having purchased her for marriage but now refusing, must provide someone else to take his place — a Hebrew, not a foreigner. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

### v. 9 — "And if he chooses her for his son, he must deal with her as with a daughter."

- If the master betroths her to his son instead of marrying her himself, she is to be treated with the full rights of a daughter — including dowry, food, clothing, and respect. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: The son must treat her "after the manner of the daughters of Israel that are virgins" — providing food, raiment, and conjugal duty. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)

### v. 10 — "If he takes another wife, he must not reduce the food, clothing, or marital rights of his first wife."

- Enduring Word: Even if the master (or his son) took another wife, the first wife's material and marital rights remained protected. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: The phrase "duty of marriage" (*`onatah*) is understood by most Jewish and Christian interpreters as conjugal rights (cf. 1 Cor 7:3). Some take it as "habitation" (a dwelling), but the majority view is marital intimacy. The Mishnah specifies set times for this duty. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott: Polygamy is "viewed as lawful in this passage, as elsewhere generally in the Mosaic Law, which did not venture to forbid, though to some extent discouraging it." The legislator allowed many things "for the hardness of their hearts" (Matt 19:8). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

### v. 11 — "If, however, he does not provide her with these three things, she is free to go without monetary payment."

- Enduring Word: If the household failed in its obligations, she was granted unconditional freedom. These were remarkable protections for a girl who had no natural protector in that society. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: The "three things" are: (1) espousing her to himself, (2) espousing her to his son, or (3) letting her be redeemed. If none of these is done, she goes free without payment. Some interpreters (rejected by Gill and Aben Ezra) take the "three" as food, clothing, and marital rights — but Gill follows the Targum of Jonathan. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)

### v. 12 — "Whoever strikes and kills a man must surely be put to death."

- Enduring Word: Capital punishment for murder goes back to Genesis 9:6, grounded in the image of God in man. The state's right to use the sword of execution is affirmed in Romans 13:3-4. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: This applies universally — "man, woman, or child, of whatsoever nation." The death penalty is by order of the civil magistrate. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott: The death penalty for murder had already received divine sanction in the Noahic covenant (Gen 9:6) and "tradition, backed up by conscience, had made it an almost universal law." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

### v. 13 — "If, however, he did not lie in wait, but God allowed it to happen, then I will appoint for you a place where he may flee."

- This distinguishes manslaughter (accidental killing) from murder. The "place" refers ultimately to the cities of refuge (Numbers 35; Joshua 20). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: "But God delivers him into his hand" — God's providence orders even what seems accidental. The manslayer flees to the camp of the Levites while in the wilderness, and later to the cities of refuge in Canaan. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott: "Hitherto, throughout the East, it had been regarded as the duty of the next of kin to avenge homicide of whatever kind… The Sinaitic legislation for the first time interposed the 'city of refuge' between the 'avenger of blood' and his victim." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

### v. 14 — "But if a man schemes and acts willfully against his neighbor to kill him, you must take him away from My altar to be put to death."

- Enduring Word: God denied murderers sanctuary at His altar. Throughout the ancient world, altars were places of refuge — but God said there is to be no mercy for premeditated murder. The principle that unpunished murders defile a land (Num 35:31-34) is "a sobering, humbling thought." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: Even if the murderer were a priest ministering at the altar, he was to be taken and executed. The Targum of Jonathan says: "though he is a priest… thou shalt take him from thence, and slay him with the sword." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott: "In most parts of the ancient world a scruple was felt about putting criminals to death when once they had taken sanctuary… The Mosaic Law regarded this scruple as a superstition, and refused to sanction it." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

### v. 15 — "Whoever strikes his father or mother must surely be put to death."

- Enduring Word: "Strikes" must be read in context with v. 12 — a child who murdered or attempted to murder a parent received capital punishment. The Law also had a built-in protection: parents could not carry out the punishment themselves but had to bring the child before the elders (Deut 21:18-21). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: The blow had to cause a bruise, weal, or mark. The Targum of Jonathan adds the method was "suffocation of a napkin" (strangulation). "This crime was made capital, to show the heinousness of it, how detestable it was to God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott: "The parent is viewed as God's representative, and to smite him is to offer God an insult in his person." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

### v. 16 — "Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession."

- Enduring Word: "Kidnapping for slavery was common in the ancient world" (Cole) and is here clearly prohibited. This is a "subtle yet important difference between slavery as it was commonly practiced and slavery as regulated in the Bible." Most ancient slavery was a form of kidnapping, but in Israel it was entered willingly. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill: This law applies to "men stealers in general," as the Apostle Paul references in 1 Tim 1:9-10. If the kidnapper was found with the victim in his hand before selling him, he was still guilty of death. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott: "Kidnapping is a crime against the person only a very little short of murder, since it is to deprive a man of that which gives life its chief value — liberty." Joseph's story (Gen 37) illustrates how easy it was to sell a free man as a slave. "The stringent law of the Mosaic code was greatly needed to check an atrocious crime very widely committed." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

### v. 17 — "Anyone who curses his father or mother must surely be put to death."

- Enduring Word: "The idea of the curse here is more like what we would think of as a death threat" (citing Cole). "To curse was to will and pray the downfall of the other with all one's heart." The law preserved a critical foundation for society: respect between generations. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Gill (implied context): This is a capital offense alongside striking parents and kidnapping. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html)
- Ellicott: "To curse him implies, if possible, a greater want of reverence; and, since curses can only be effectual as appeals to God, it is an attempt to enlist God on our side against His representative." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

### vv. 18–19 — "If men are quarreling and one strikes the other with a stone or a fist… confined to bed… then the one who struck him shall go unpunished, as long as the other can get up and walk around outside with his staff. Nevertheless, he must compensate the man for his lost work and see that he is completely healed."

- Enduring Word: This is personal injury law. If the injured man recovered enough to walk with a staff, the assailant was acquitted of a capital charge but had to pay for lost time and medical expenses. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Ellicott: Retaliation ("eye for eye") could not practically be applied here without risking killing the man, which would be excessive. Therefore a fine was imposed to compensate for lost time and medical costs. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- Gill: Jewish writers added that the assailant also had to pay for pain and for loss of any member. The compensation covered "as much as he could have got in that time by his labour." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-21.html, via excerpt)

### vv. 20–21 — "If a man strikes his manservant or maidservant with a rod, and the servant dies by his hand, he shall surely be punished. However, if the servant gets up after a day or two, the owner shall not be punished, since the servant is his property."

- Enduring Word: "This shows that in ancient Israel servants could be murdered. In many other cultures, the master was held blameless if he murdered a servant." The great advance is that the slave "is considered here as a person" (Cole). If the servant lingered a day or two and then died, the master was not subject to the death penalty — the loss of the servant was considered his own financial punishment ("he is his money"). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Ellicott: "Unlike most other codes, it proceeded to forbid the homicide of slaves. Hitherto, throughout the East... slaves had been regarded as so absolutely their master's property that he was entitled to do as he pleased with them." The exact penalty is debated: Talmud says death; some modern Jews say a fine. The proviso in v. 21 presumes that if death is not immediate, it was not intended — and the master already suffers by losing his own property. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- **The Expositor's Bible Commentary**: "Moses excelled the legislators of Greece and Rome, by making an assault or chastisement which killed him upon the spot as worthy of death as if a freeman had been slain. It was only the victim who lingered that died comparatively unavenged." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/exodus-21.html)
- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary**: If the slave died directly from the beating, the master was punished. If the slave survived a day or two before dying, the master was not punished — but neither could he replace the slave; "he had to bear the cost of the loss." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-21.html)

### v. 22 — "If men who are fighting strike a pregnant woman and her child is born prematurely, but there is no further injury, he shall surely be fined as the woman's husband demands and as the court allows."

- Enduring Word: "This is an example of a case of retribution, where a pregnant woman was injured in a conflict, and she gave birth prematurely. A penalty was only to be assessed if there was lasting damage." The fine was assessed by the husband and the judges. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Ellicott: The miscarriage is assumed to be accidental — the pregnant wife intervening in her husband's quarrel. "And yet no mischief follow — i.e., no further mischief — nothing beyond the loss of the child." If the woman herself died, the death penalty applied (v. 23). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- **Keil & Delitzsch**: "A pecuniary compensation was to be paid, such as the husband of the woman laid upon him, and he was to give it by (by an appeal to) arbitrators. A fine is imposed, because even if no injury had been done to the woman and the fruit of her womb, such a blow might have endangered life." The plural "children" (*yeladeyha*) is used because there might be more than one child in the womb. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-21.html, via excerpt)

### vv. 23–25 — "But if a serious injury results, then you must require a life for a life — eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, and stripe for stripe."

- This is the *lex talionis* (law of retaliation). All traditional sources stress it was a *limitation* on revenge, not a license for it.
- Enduring Word: "This law was meant to block man's natural desire for vengeance. It was not given as a license for revenge." Our natural tendency is to want to do more to the offender than they did to us. This principle "can apply to our modern practice of assessing huge punitive damages in lawsuits." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Ellicott: "It is a reasonable conjecture that the law of retaliation was much older than Moses, and accepted by him as tolerable rather than devised as rightful." Aristotle says the Pythagoreans approved it. "Theoretically, retaliation is the exactest and strictest justice; but in practice difficulties arise." The present passage "sanctioned the law of retaliation in principle, but authorised its enforcement in a single case only." Later, Lev 24:17-21 and Deut 19:21 applied it universally. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- **The Expositor's Bible Commentary** (quoting Augustine, *Cont. Faust.* xix.25): "This command was not given for exciting the fires of hatred, but to restrain them. For who would easily be satisfied with repaying as much injury as he received? … Upon this immoderate and unjust vengeance, the law imposed a just limit, not that what was quenched might be kindled, but that what was burning might not spread." The commentary also notes that the Jews learned to commute this to money compensation by reasoning from the principle itself. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/exodus-21.html)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: Jesus referred to this principle in Matt 5:38 and "pronounced a higher law, that of mercy toward the offender." It also notes a practical problem: "It would be manifestly unjust to require an 'eye for an eye' in the case of a one-eyed man!" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-21.html)

### vv. 26–27 — "If a man strikes and blinds the eye of his manservant or maidservant, he must let the servant go free as compensation for the eye. And if he knocks out the tooth… he must let the servant go free as compensation for the tooth."

- Enduring Word: The *lex talionis* had a different application for slaves. A master who destroyed a servant's eye or knocked out a tooth had to set the servant free — which was "something more precious than an eye — his freedom." This gave masters incentive to treat servants as people, not work-animals. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Ellicott: An exception to the law of retaliation is made because the marked social inequality would make exact retaliation unjust. The master "loses all property in his slave, and is bound at once to emancipate him." The loss of an eye is the greatest permanent injury; the loss of a tooth the least — both result in freedom. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- **Keil & Delitzsch**: "The *lex talionis* applied to the free Israelite only, not to slaves. In the case of the latter, if the master struck out an eye… or struck out a tooth, he was to let him go free, as a compensation for the loss of the member." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-21.html)
- **Whedon's Commentary** (Methodist): The male or female servant "was reckoned as not enjoying the same natural rights as freemen. The *lex talionis* did not apply to them, but they were allowed their freedom as a compensation." But these provisions "must have tended to mitigate the wrongs of slavery, and protect the lives and persons of slaves, in a way unknown to the laws and customs of other ancient nations." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-21.html)

### v. 28 — "If an ox gores a man or woman to death, the ox must surely be stoned, and its meat must not be eaten. But the owner of the ox shall not be held responsible."

- Enduring Word: This law illustrates the principle of intent and neglect. An owner of a man-killing ox could not be held guilty if the animal had no history of aggression. Yet the animal must die and the owner could not profit from it (its flesh not eaten). "No one was to profit from or regard casually even accidental death." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Ellicott: The ox dies the death of a murderer. Its flesh may not be eaten because an animal killed by stoning would not be properly bled (unclean for Hebrews). According to the Rabbis, the flesh could not even be sold to Gentiles but had to be buried — "to mark strongly that whatever creature took human life was accursed." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary**: "The animal that killed him was destroyed as in the case of an animal that killed a free person. This destruction of the animal was a recognition of the sanctity of human life." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-21.html)

### vv. 29–30 — "But if the ox has a habit of goring, and its owner has been warned yet does not restrain it… the ox must be stoned and its owner must also be put to death. If payment is demanded of him instead, he may redeem his life by paying the full amount demanded of him."

- Enduring Word: The law distinguishes between negligence and innocence. If the owner knew the ox was dangerous and did nothing, he was held guilty of murder. However, the death penalty could be commuted to a ransom payment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Ellicott: The owner was "liable to a process for murder; but, with the consent of the aggrieved family, might pay a sum of money as compensation instead." The amount was "whatsoever is laid upon him" — primarily by the aggrieved relatives, but with appeal to the judges if the demand was exorbitant. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

### vv. 31–32 — "If the ox gores a son or a daughter, it shall be done to him according to the same rule. If the ox gores a manservant or maidservant, the owner must pay thirty shekels of silver to the master of that servant, and the ox must be stoned."

- Enduring Word: The same principles applied whether the victim was a free son/daughter or a slave — with the difference that for a slave, the compensation went to the slave's master, at the fixed rate of thirty shekels (the standard price of a slave; cf. Lev 27:3). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Ellicott: "In the case of a slave, the sum was fixed at what was regarded as the standard price of a slave… viz., thirty silver shekels." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary**: "If the person killed by the animal was a slave, compensation was paid to the master, since he owned the slave. But the slave was acknowledged as a human being, not treated as a mere 'thing,' and the animal that killed him was destroyed." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-21.html)

### vv. 33–34 — "If a man opens or digs a pit and fails to cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the pit shall make restitution; he must pay its owner, and the dead animal will be his."

- Enduring Word: This law deals with negligence. The one who created a hazard (an uncovered pit) bore responsibility for resulting damage. He paid the full value of the live animal and then kept the carcass. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Ellicott: In the East, wells commonly have covers removed when water is drawn and then replaced. If a man neglected to replace a cover — or dug a new well and left it uncovered — he was answerable. "Having paid the full value of the live animal, the owner of the well was entitled to make what he could by the carcass." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

### v. 35 — "If a man's ox injures his neighbor's ox and it dies, they must sell the live one and divide the proceeds; they also must divide the dead animal."

- Both share the loss equally when neither owner was at fault (the ox had no prior history of goring). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Ellicott: "Where no blame attached to the owner, the loss was to be equally shared." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

### v. 36 — "But if it was known that the ox had a habit of goring, yet its owner failed to restrain it, he shall pay full compensation, ox for ox, and the dead animal will be his."

- If the owner knew his ox was dangerous and failed to restrain it, he bore the full loss — paying "ox for ox" (full replacement value), and keeping the dead animal. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Ellicott: "Where the dangerous character of the animal was, or ought to have been, known, the man whose ox was killed received its full value." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)

## Denominational Distinctives & Points of Tension

### On Slavery (vv. 2–11)

There is broad agreement across all traditions consulted that the Mosaic Law did not institute slavery but regulated an existing institution and humanised it. **Spurgeon** (Baptist/Reformed), quoted by David Guzik: "Moses did not institute slavery in any shape; the laws concerning it were made on purpose to repress it." The **Expositor's Bible Commentary** (Anglican/evangelical strand) similarly states: "a denunciation of all slavery would have been premature, and therefore unwise; but assuredly the germs of emancipation were already planted." **Whedon's Commentary** (Methodist) likewise emphasises the protective tendency. No substantial denominational divide emerged in the sources on this question — all read these laws as restrictive and ameliorative rather than prescriptive of slavery. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/exodus-21.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/exodus-21.html)

### On the "Eye for Eye" Principle (vv. 23–25) and Jesus' Teaching

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** explicitly contrasts Jesus' higher law of mercy (Matt 5:38) with the Mosaic *lex talionis*. It notes the practical difficulty of literal application (e.g., a one-eyed man). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/exodus-21.html)
- **The Expositor's Bible Commentary** (citing Augustine) frames the *lex talionis* as a *restraint* on vengeance, preparing for a higher morality. It notes that the Jews themselves learned to commute it to money payments. Jesus "plainly means to instruct private persons not to exact their rights, whereas the magistrate continues to be 'a revenger to execute justice.'" This is a common Reformed/Anglican distinction between personal ethics and civil justice. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/exodus-21.html)
- **Enduring Word** (Pentecostal/charismatic, David Guzik) treats the law primarily as a limitation on revenge, not contradicting but consistent with Jesus' teaching — Jesus addressed personal vengeance, while the law addressed judicial sentencing. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary**: Jesus "did not contradict the principle of fair punishment for wrongdoing, a principle that is a basic element in civil government. Jesus was not laying down laws for civil administrators as was the case with Moses, but was reminding his disciples that they must not always stand on their rights." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/exodus-21.html)

### On Exodus 21:22 and the Abortion Debate

- This is a major point of modern controversy not fully developed in the older commentaries consulted. **Ellicott** reads "her fruit depart from her" as miscarriage, with a fine imposed for the loss of the child but death penalty only if the mother died — implying the fetus was not treated as a full human life under the *lex talionis*. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
- **Keil & Delitzsch** treat "if injury occur" as potentially to "the mother or the child," with "soul for soul" applying in either case — implying the child's life was protected equally. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/exodus-21.html, via excerpt)
- **Enduring Word** (David Guzik) reads "gives birth prematurely" (BSB/NIV rendering) and applies the *lex talionis* only "if lasting damage resulted" — focusing on injury to the mother or the surviving child. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-21/)
- Note: The BSB (Berean Standard Bible) uses "born prematurely," which differs from the KJV "depart from her," creating a translation-dependent interpretive difference. ### On Polygamy (v. 10)

**Ellicott** notes frankly that polygamy "is viewed as lawful in this passage, as elsewhere generally in the Mosaic Law, which did not venture to forbid, though to some extent discouraging it. The legislator was forced to allow many things to the Hebrews, 'for the hardness of their hearts' (Matthew 19:8)." This is the standard traditional reading across denominations. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/21.htm)
